newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Annan wants rights mission in Zaire to "get facts".
newsitem.headline: Annan wants rights mission in Zaire to "get facts".

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan indicated on Thursday he would give way to demands by Congo that he drop the chief of a team to investigate alleged massacres in the country, if it cleared the way for the probe to go ahead.

Annan said difficult negotiations continued in Kinshasa over the terms for the U.N. investigation, due to start on Monday, including whether the team should include Chilean lawyer Roberto Garreton, U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the renamed Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In April, Garreton accused rebel troops of Laurent Kabila -- who has since become president of the former Zaire -- of massacring Rwandan refugees during their push across eastern Zaire in 1996. His latest report is due out in the next several days, U.N. officials said.
Annan, asked whether he had dropped Garreton from the team, told reporters in Geneva: "I think we all have to be realistic and practical.
"We have a team led by Garreton. Ideally, we would want them to continue. If that doesn't happen we are not going to let them (the government) use that to prevent us from getting to the facts.

"The rule of law and primacy of law does not mean one has to be rigid and inflexible. In our own countries it is not unusual sometimes for the accused to request a change of judge, a change of venue or other things.
"I think we should not let our desire for purity get in the way of doing the right thing and getting to the facts. And we will get to the facts."
He recalled a pledge by President Kabila in June to allow the probe to proceed and determine whether his troops had massacred Rwandan Hutus.
"I would hope that he will give us the support, the access and the cooperation of the government that we need to do a credible investigation," Annan said.
"The most important thing is for us to get to the facts," he added. "The alleged mass killings ought to be investigated."
Kabila's Tutsi-dominated Alliance forces overthrew then president Mobutu Sese Seko in May.
Kabila has denied the massacre allegations, but his authorities have blocked attempts to go ahead with the probe, authorised in April by the 53-member U.N. Human Rights Commission.
A U.N. advance team including Argentine forensic experts who would excavate suspected mass graves has been in Kinshasa for two weeks.

Some U.N. officials said they feared the dropping of Garreton could set a dangerous precedent and undermine U.N. special rapporteurs investigating alleged abuses in 16 countries including Burma, Iraq, and Nigeria.
Annan, on a five-day visit to the U.N.'s European headquarters, said: "If we were drop the investigation altogether then the government would have won.
"If we persist and get to the facts and take the action necessary once we have the facts and send the message out that impunity is not acceptable, I think it is much more important."

Other sticking points include a government demand that the group investigate atrocities against refugees that may have occurred before October 1996, before Kabila's allies became active in eastern Zaire.
The U.N. team is also seeking guarantees of freedom of movement to travel to sites of alleged mass graves.
